- Map strategies to concrete actions and verify against constraints (e.g., interval choice, box selection).
- Always double-check that final probability is worst-case, not just average-case, and that the solution holds for all possible number arrangements.
- Avoid overcomplicating: maximize minimal probability via symmetry and randomness when relevant.
knowledge: Minimax / worst-case probability: interpret the task as finding the largest p such that for every configuration (adversarial choice) of 20 distinct nonnegative reals, Alice can employ a (possibly randomized) strategy that guarantees success probability at least p.
Randomized strategies and symmetry: randomization over which boxes to open or which closed box to guess is allowed and often used to equalize success probabilities across adversarial placements.

Combinatorics / enumeration of actions: Alice may open any strict subset of the 20 boxes (i.e., 0 to 19 boxes) and then must choose one closed box to guess; feasible strategies are constrained by which boxes remain closed.

Intervals and boundedness: Alice's guess must be a bounded (finite) interval. This forbids using unbounded intervals (e.g., [0,∞)) to trivially guarantee success, so interval-width and placement matter.

Information limits from opening boxes: opening up to 19 boxes reveals their exact values but does not reveal the closed box's value; that partial information must be converted into an interval-guess that works with high worst-case probability.

Analogy to optimal stopping/selection ideas: the trace references problems like the secretary problem to motivate considering sampling and randomized selection, but here the objective and constraints differ (bounded-interval guess, adversarial values).
constraints_instructions: There are exactly 20 boxes, each contains a distinct real number ≥ 0.
Alice may open any strict subset of the boxes (i.e., she may open 0 through 19 boxes) but she may not open all 20.
After opening, she must choose one closed box and submit a single bounded interval (finite endpoints) as her guess; the guess succeeds iff that box's number lies in the submitted interval.

The strategy may be randomized; success probability is measured over the strategy's randomness, and p must be guaranteed for every possible placement of the 20 numbers (worst-case / minimax requirement).
The goal is to maximize the guaranteed minimal success probability p (the value must be independent of the actual numbers).
Do not use unbounded intervals (they are disallowed by the problem statement).
Cautions: do not assume any prior distribution on numbers; do not assume opening boxes yields the closed box's value; ensure any claimed guarantee truly holds for every adversarial configuration.
approach: Perspective: treat the task as a minimax ordering/interval-selection problem under an adversary who fixes 20 distinct nonnegative reals; Alice’s randomness is the only source of unpredictability. Strategy outline: randomize which strict subset of boxes to open (choose a distribution on closed sets), observe the opened values, then pick one closed box and submit a single bounded interval determined from the observed order statistics. Core concepts and guiding principles: (1) symmetry and randomization — use uniform or symmetric random choices over boxes to make every adversarial placement have equal or nearly equal success probability; (2) order-statistics exploitation — after opening boxes use the observed minima/maxima and adjacencies to place a tight bounded interval that captures closed-box values whenever they fall between observed neighbors; (3) information-versus-choice tradeoff — opening more boxes increases information but leaves fewer closed targets to choose from; leaving multiple closed boxes can be beneficial because you may be able to select one of them after seeing the opened values; (4) combinatorial worst-case accounting — translate any candidate randomized protocol into a combinatorial probability that the adversary can force failure (e.g., all closed boxes occupying adversarial extreme positions) and maximize p by minimizing that failure-count. Problem-solving philosophy: design simple, symmetric randomized protocols (choose a random closed subset size m and/or random closed indices), characterize failure events purely by ranks (where closed boxes fall among the 1..20 order positions), compute the minimal success probability p for that protocol by counting rank-configurations, then optimize over m and the randomization to maximize the guaranteed p. Operational checks: ensure all guessed intervals are finite, verify the bound holds for every adversarial placement (no distributional assumptions), and prefer protocols whose failure cases are few and symmetric so the combinatorial bound is tight and analyzable.

plan.step: 1. Formalize the objective as a minimax problem and set notation.

rationale.Knowledge: Treat p as the largest value such that for every fixed configuration of 20 distinct nonnegative reals, Alice has a randomized strategy guaranteeing success probability ≥ p.
rationale.Constraints_Instructions: The strategy may randomize; success is worst-case over placements; intervals must be bounded; Alice may open 0..19 boxes but not all 20.
rationale.Approach: Make the adversary/strategy roles explicit so later counting and rank-based arguments map directly to success probabilities.

plan.step: 2. Reduce the problem to ranks/order-statistics of the 20 numbers.

rationale.Knowledge: Only relative order (ranks) matters for whether a bounded interval based on observed values captures an unobserved value.
rationale.Constraints_Instructions: Numbers are distinct, so each box has a unique rank 1..20; opening boxes reveals exact values and thus their ranks among opened ones.
rationale.Approach: Rephrase events (success/failure) in terms of where the chosen closed box's rank lies relative to observed ranks; this simplifies combinatorial counting of success cases.

plan.step: 3. Exhibit a simple candidate strategy that attains a high guaranteed probability: open 19 boxes, leave one box chosen uniformly at random closed; after opening, guess the interval [min(observed), max(observed)].

rationale.Knowledge: With 19 observed values, the interval between their min and max is a bounded interval determined from observations.
rationale.Constraints_Instructions: Opening 19 boxes is allowed (strict subset), and the interval [min,max] is finite — thus valid.
rationale.Approach: Use symmetry/randomization (uniformly random omitted box) to make success probability equal to the fraction of positions (ranks) that fall inside the observed min–max, which is easy to count.

plan.step: 4. Compute the guaranteed success probability of that candidate strategy.

rationale.Knowledge: If the omitted box is not the global minimum or maximum, its value lies between some observed values and hence inside [min(observed), max(observed)].
rationale.Constraints_Instructions: There are 20 possible boxes to omit (strategy randomizes uniformly); failures occur exactly when the omitted box is the global min or global max.
rationale.Approach: Count failures: 2 bad ranks out of 20, so success probability = 1 - 2/20 = 18/20 = 9/10 for every fixed configuration.

plan.step: 5. Prove optimality: show no strategy can guarantee probability > 18/20.

rationale.Knowledge: An adversary can place two 'extreme' values so that any bounded-interval guess fails when the chosen closed box is at those extreme ranks unless the strategy can deterministically identify them without opening all boxes (which is impossible).
rationale.Constraints_Instructions: Alice cannot open all 20 boxes, so for any randomized protocol there remain choices of a closed box unknown to Alice; intervals must be finite and chosen after seeing opened boxes.
rationale.Approach: Formal adversarial construction: fix any strategy (possibly randomized). The adversary places two values extremely small and extremely large compared to the others. For whichever closed-box index the strategy leaves/chooses, at least those two extreme ranks can be made to lie outside any bounded interval the player might output, so for the fixed configuration the strategy fails on at least 2 of the 20 possible omitted-box positions; thus worst-case success ≤ 18/20.

plan.step: 6. Conclude and verify compliance with all problem constraints.

rationale.Knowledge: Combining the achievable lower bound (step 4) and the upper bound (step 5) identifies the exact minimax value.
rationale.Constraints_Instructions: Verify the proposed protocol uses only allowed actions (opens ≤19 boxes, outputs a finite interval) and that the adversarial upper bound respects the worst-case requirement.
rationale.Approach: Conclude p* = 18/20 = 9/10, and state that this value is tight because the explicit strategy achieves it and no strategy can exceed it under the given constraints.

summary.knowledge: Minimax view: find the largest p such that for every adversarial placement of 20 distinct nonnegative reals Alice (possibly randomized) guarantees success ≥ p. Randomization and symmetry are tools to equalize success across placements. Alice may open any strict subset (0–19) and then must pick one closed box and submit a bounded (finite) interval. Opening boxes reveals order-statistic information but not the closed value. The problem resembles selection/secretary ideas but with adversarial values and bounded-interval guesses.
summary.constraints_instructions: 20 boxes, distinct reals ≥0. Alice may open any strict subset (0–19 boxes) but not all 20. After observing opened values she must choose one closed box and submit a finite interval; success iff that box's number lies in the interval. Strategies may be randomized; p is the worst-case (min over placements) success probability guaranteed by the strategy. Do not use unbounded intervals or assume any prior distribution; proofs must hold for every adversarial placement.
summary.approach: Minimax over ranks: randomize which boxes remain closed (or choose random closed-set size m), observe opened values' order statistics, then select a closed box and place a finite interval determined from adjacent observed ranks. Use symmetry to make failure events uniform and count rank-configurations to compute worst-case success probability; optimize the randomization (e.g., m and distribution on closed indices) to maximize the guaranteed p. Always verify interval finiteness and adversarial robustness.

task:
Which of these Turing Machines halts after the most number of steps and what is the number of steps (initial tape is empty - all zero):
1) B1L B0R C1R E0L A1L D0R C0R A1R C1L H1L
2) B1L C1R C1L B1L D1L E0R A1R D1R H1L A0R
3) B1L A1L C1R B1R A1L D1R A1L E1R H1L C0R
agent_planning:
1. Parse the question and extract all labels representing the Turing Machines, their transition rules, and the halting criteria.
2. Determine that solving this requires simulating the execution of each candidate Turing Machine (TM) from an initially blank tape and counting steps until a halt state is reached.
3. For each TM, break down the transition strings (e.g., B1L) to extract: current state, symbol read, symbol written, move direction, next state.
4. Decide that the most efficient tool is code execution, since the TMs must be faithfully simulated for up to tens of millions of steps.
5. Structure a simulation engine:
   a. Convert the compact notation into a transition table for each TM.
   b. For each TM, initialize tape (all zeros), head position (usually at the leftmost cell), and starting state (probably 'A').
   c. Iteratively apply the transition rules: read symbol, write symbol, move, update state, increment a step counter.
   d. Halt when reaching the designated halting state (e.g., 'H').
6. Implement bookkeeping to track the exact number of steps per machine.
7. Compare the results: for each TM, extract its associated halting step count. Determine which halts after the most steps, and store both the TM index and its step count.
8. Output the final answer as specified.

No Search Agent needed. All computation is by the Code Agent.

knowledge: Turing machine (TM) fundamentals: a TM has a finite set of states (including a start state and a halting state), a (bi-)infinite tape of symbols, a head that reads/writes a symbol and moves left or right, and a transition function mapping (state, read symbol) to (write symbol, move direction, next state).

Simulation mechanics: to determine halting behavior and step counts, you must iteratively apply the transition rules from an initial configuration until a halting state is reached, counting each transition as one step.

Representation and parsing: the compact transition notation (e.g., strings like 'B1L' or similar) must be parsed into the five components: current state, symbol read, symbol to write, direction to move, and next state. Understanding how the given encoding maps into those components is required.

Initial conditions and conventions: the tape is initially blank (a designated blank symbol or '0'), the head starts at a specified cell (commonly the leftmost or a central cell), and the start state is typically 'A' unless another start state is stated.

Data structures and algorithms: use a dynamic tape representation (e.g., hash/dictionary for sparse infinite tape or a resizable array) and a transition table (map/dict keyed by (state,symbol)) for O(1) rule lookup per step.

Practical considerations: simulation may require tens of millions of steps, so efficient state lookups, minimal per-step overhead, and integer step counters are necessary; also be ready to detect undefined transitions (treated as halting if specified) and avoid unbounded memory growth by storing only non-blank cells.

task:

What is the dimension of the log blowup of $P$ in $I$?

approach: Perspective: Work purely in the toric/log-combinatorial language: treat P = Spec(k, N^3) as affine 3-space with the standard fine log structure so monoid generators correspond to variables x,y,z. Strategy: translate the log ideal I generated by (1,0,0) and (0,1,0) into the monomial ideal (x,y), model the log blowup as the toric subdivision of the positive orthant cone in R^3 induced by that monomial ideal, and read the geometry from the resulting cones/monoids. Core concepts and guiding principles: (1) log blowups of toric/fine-monoid charts are computed combinatorially by subdividing cones and introducing new rays corresponding to generators of the ideal; (2) each maximal cone of the subdivision gives an affine chart whose coordinate ring is the monoid algebra of the dual cone, so scheme-theoretic (Krull) dimension equals the rank of the associated lattice/monoid; (3) the strict transform and exceptional loci are visible combinatorially as faces/cones removed or replaced by lower-rank pieces. Problem-solving steps (concise and tool-minimal): (a) identify monomials x,y (from (1,0,0),(0,1,0)) inside k[N^3]≃k[x,y,z]; (b) form the subdivision of the positive orthant cone induced by the monomial ideal (intuitively inserting the ray(s) that separate e1 and e2 directions), record the resulting maximal cones and their monoids; (c) write the affine charts as k[monoid] for each maximal cone and compute their Krull dimensions (equivalently read off the rank of the cone/monoid); (d) inspect the strict transform/exceptional cones to determine whether any chart’s dimension drops; (e) conclude the blowup dimension from the chart dimensions and give a short combinatorial justification. Constraints respected: no external search, use only combinatorial/elementary algebraic manipulation, keep computations explicit and minimal, and present the final dimension with a brief combinatorial justification based on the chart/cone analysis.
